seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: I hope you are not ill with this bad epidemic as it is a long time since I heard from you. I am glad to say we are all well and I trust all with you are the same. The above is my new address. It was rather difficult to find quarters but luckily (through my milkman) I got rooms in the same street.

I sent you lately the 8th episode (Lestrygonians) and before that the 7th (Eolus) but have had no acknowledgment of receipt. Miss Weaver wrote lately and said that she had not received this episode from you. I hope to be able to send you the ninth episode (Scylla and Carybdis) shortly. Enclosed are some extra press notices of my former book. Molto fumo e poco arrosto for only 40 copies seem to have been sold this year. I should be pleased to receive from you copies of the Little Review for August, September and October. I hope the chapters have appeared intact.

I sent you also a presentation copy of Exiles which I hope you got. I wrote once or twice to Yeats and to Mr Sturge Moore about its production but have received no reply. My agent (at my request) sent copies also to Pioneer Players and to Miss Horniman. No reply. I have heard nothing from my publisher in New York either as to the sales of this book or the press notices in America or its production there. I should like to put the play into the hands of some active agent. A Mr Marion L Bloom wrote to me a long time ago but my illness made me forget his proposal. The name is rather curious, is it not? But so many of these strange coincidences happen. Whether he would like to take on the representation for Ulysses is I suppose doubtful. Messrs Crès and Co , Boul’ S. Germain, have placed their printer at the disposal of my publisher whoever or wherever he be when and if Ulysses is published.

Miss Weaver wrote that a Mr Fels wanted to do a French translation. It will appear I presume together with Mr Davray’s article . I wrote also to Mr Linati about an Italian version and a Miss Maag wrote about a Danish translation. I had also a letter from Mr George Brandes asking for a copy of the book. I had none to send him.

My delay in sending you Exiles is due to the slowness of my publisher in forwarding copies. But perhaps transit of books is long and difficult. I think you do not admire the play but perhaps you will accept it in the way I mean it.
With kind regards to Mrs Pound and yourself from us all and best wishes for your continued good health

postscript.p: P.S. I have received a letter from a Mr Owen Nugent, 2 Carnmore Terrace, Whiterock road, Belfast. He has read the first episode of Ulysses and likes it. If you send him a copy of the second perhaps he may wish to subscribe to your review. I think he will if he is not already a subscriber.

div.note: The influenza pandemic of 1918–1919, known as the Spanish flu, was reaching a peak at this time. Between February 1918 to April 1920, it infected 500 million people in successive waves, and was responsible for 20 million deaths or more.
In October 1918, JJ and family had moved from Universitätstrasse 38 to Universitätstrasse 29, where they remained until October 1919.

note.p: JJ had sent “Aeolus,” the seventh episode of Ulysses, to Pound in mid-August 1918 and “Lestrygonians,” the eighth episode, in mid-October, with requests that he provide a copy to Harriet Shaw Weaver for publication in the London magazine Egoist. Pound was foreign editor of the New York magazine Little Review at this time and was actively publishing work by JJ and other modernist figures. “Aeolus” appeared in The Little Review, vol. 5, no. 6 (October 1918): 26-51. “Lestrygonians” appeared in two numbers of The Little Review, vol. 5, nos. 9-10/11 (January and February-March 1919): 27-50, 58-62. For these episodes, see JJ to Pound, 28 August 1918, notes.

Replying to this letter of JJ’s on 22 November 1918, Pound was effusive in his praise for the recent Bloom episodes: “Bloom is a great man, and you have almightily answered the critics who asked me whether having made Stephen, more or less autobiography, you could ever go on and create a second character. ‘Second character is the test’ etc. etc., jab jab jobber-jabble” (Pound/Joyce 145).

div.note: “Scylla and Charybdis,” the ninth episode of Ulysses, appeared in two numbers of The Little Review, vol. 5, no. 12-vol. 6, no. 1 (April and May 1919): 30-43, 17-35. For this episode, see JJ to Pound, 28 August 1918, notes.

The Italian “molto fumo e poco arrosto” (literally, “much smoke and little roast”) expresses JJ’s disappointment at slow sales after strong critical reviews of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, published in its first English edition from English sheets by the Egoist Ltd. in March 1918. It had previously been published in New York by B.W. Huebsch in December 1916 and in a first English edition from American sheets in February 1917 (John J. Slocum and Herbert Cahoon, A Bibliography of James Joyce [New Haven: Yale University Press, 1953], 18-21).

As foreign editor of The Little Review, Pound had overseen serial publication of episodes of Ulysses beginning in March 1918. The August issue, which was a “Henry James Number,” was mostly taken up with essays on James by Pound and others, and did not include a Ulysses installment. The September number included “Hades” (15-37), and the October number “Aeolus” (26-51). JJ was upset over Pound’s excision of several potentially controversial passages from the fourth episode, “Calypso” – including those rendering Leopold Bloom’s morning defecation – especially as JJ had insisted that his episodes be published without changes. “Calypso” appeared in The Little Review, vol. 5, no. 2 (June 1918): 39-52. For that episode, see JJ to Pound, 9 April 1918, notes.

JJ’s Exiles was published by Grant Richards in London and by B.W. Huebsch in New York in May 1918. Pound’s support for Exiles was reserved: “a play perhaps unstageable, but infinitely more worth staging than the inanities which the once active Stage Society now indulges in” (The Future, vol. 2, no. 11 [November 1918]: 286–87).

JJ put much energy into attempting to get Exiles produced for the stage. W.B. Yeats (1865–1939) had rejected it for the Dublin Abbey Theatre in August 1917 (LII 405). As a member of the Incorporated Stage Society in London, Thomas Sturge Moore (1870–1944), writer, translator, and artist, supported the staging of Exiles; but JJ, after losing patience with the Society’s protracted indecision, withdrew the play from consideration (see JJ to Pound, 5 June 1917, notes; and 9 July 1917, notes). London’s Pioneer Players (1911–1925) were known for presenting controversial, noncommercial plays. Annie Horniman (1860–1937) was a prominent and wealthy supporter of modern Irish and English theatre. However, the Pioneer Players never staged the play (see JJ to Pound, 30 March 1917, notes). Exiles premiered in Munich (translated into German as Verbannte) on 7 August 1919. The Stage Society finally presented it in English at London’s Regent Theatre on 14 and 15 February 1926, with W.G. Fay as director.

Marion L. Bloom (1891-1975) was a New York literary agent who wrote JJ on 4 May 1917, asking to represent him in the United States and signing herself “Marionne L. Bloom,” possibly to disguise her gender (The Cornell Joyce Collection: A Catalogue, ed. Robert E. Scholes [Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1961], 74). JJ was struck by the coincidence with the given name, Marion, of his character Molly Bloom. Marion Bloom was born in rural Maryland and met H.L. Mencken in Baltimore in 1914. She wrote stories and sketches which Mencken published in his magazine The Smart Set, and became his lover for a number of years. Several months after opening her literary agency in New York in early 1917, she joined the Army Nursing Corps and saw service in France. She also acted for some years as secretary to Theodore Dreiser. See Michael Groden, “‘Please, Mr. Postman’: Joyce’s Expanding Epistolary Novel,” in Joyce’s Non-Fiction Writings: “Outside His Jurisfiction”, ed. Katherine Ebury and James Alexander Fraser (London: Palgrave Macmillan, 2018), 31-54; In Defense of Marion: The Love of Marion Bloom and H.L. Mencken, ed. Edward A. Martin (Athens: University of Georgia Press, 1996).
G. Crès et Cie, a Parisian publisher of art and literature (see JJ to Pound, 9 April 1918, notes).

JJ’s London literary agent J.B. Pinker had given permission to Florent Fels (1891–1977), French publisher, journalist, and author, to publish a French translation of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man in Fels’s journal Action: Cahiers de philosophie et d’art (LI 120; The Cornell Joyce Collection, 69-70). Candidates for translator were, first, Louis Bagnan (LII 450), then Ludmila Savitzky (LI 142), but Fels produced only a review of the book in Action, no. 6 (December 1920): 63–64. The translation by Savitzky (1881-1957) was published as Dedalus by the Paris house, Éditions de La Sirène, in 1924.

The hint of bitterness here reflects JJ’s frustration at promises of reviews, translations, and other assistance that he did not see materializing. Henry D. Davray (1873-1944), a French critic who contributed regularly on English literature to the Mercure de France, finally published his generous remarks about JJ’s Exiles and other writings in “Lettres anglaises,” Mercure de France, vol. 121, no. 495 (1 February 1919): 512-18. See JJ to Pound, 24 July 1917, notes.

Carlo Linati (1878–1949), Italian writer and translator of English fiction. Impressed with his translations of J.M. Synge and W.B. Yeats, JJ invited him on 31 October 1918 to translate A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man into Italian (LI 121). Linati turned him down but translated Exiles instead as Esuli and published it in Il Convegno, vol.1, nos. 3-5 (April, May, June 1920): 27-52, 27-46, 22–37.

Maja Maag, in Hellerup, Denmark, had written JJ circa July 1918 that she was considering translating A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man into Danish (LI 116). A Portrait was translated into Danish by Ove Brusendorff and published as Portræt af kunstneren som ungt menneske (Copenhagen: Athenaeum Dansk Forlag, 1941).

Georg Brandes (1842–1927), distinguished Danish critic and scholar who was a pioneer in the Scandinavian naturalistic movement known as the “Modern Breakthrough,” and whose ideas influenced Henrik Ibsen. JJ greatly admired Brandes and wrote him on 6 January 1919 that he had had a copy of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man sent to him, an earlier copy having gone astray (Ellmann, JJ 230 n.).

The first and second episodes of Ulysses – “Telemachus” and “Nestor” – were printed in the March and April 1918 numbers of The Little Review, respectively. “Owen Nugent” was a pseudonym sometimes used by Percy Beaumont Wadsworth (1895-1983), a Yorkshire-born freelance journalist and foreign correspondent who lived in Ireland, India, Prague, and other countries. Pound had written JJ on 17 July 1918 that he had heard from “a friend of yrs called Wadsworth alias (??) forget,” adding that he had sent the young man some copies of The Little Review containing Ulysses and received back a selection of his creative efforts: “disjecta membra, groping in yr. vestiges” (Pound/Joyce 144). Wadsworth wrote JJ on 13 October 1918 in praise of “Telemachus,” and wrote again on 20 January 1919 to thank JJ for a photo he had sent, “which makes you look anything but Irish” (The Cornell Joyce Collection, 143-44). Dorothy Richardson, who called him “Owen,” corresponded with him often and acknowledged on 16 May 1919 receiving copies of The Little Review from him (Berg). Wadsworth later wrote “Prague Letter” for The Dial, vol. 73, no. 6 (December 1922): 655-58, and contributed to Close-Up and other periodicals during the 1920s and 1930s. Wadsworth was one of the earliest subscribers to the first edition of Ulysses; JJ inscribed a copy of the first edition for him in Paris in 1924. Many years later, Wadsworth published “Visits with James Joyce,” James Joyce Quarterly, vol. 1, no. 4 (Summer 1964): 14-18.
